title: Know what you sing
hookLine: a ragged man walks into a king's sacrifice and stops the singers cold: do you know what you're singing to?
carry: the sama veda: sacred song, sung knowing what it means

lines: A RAGGED MAN AT THE KING'S RITE.
"DO YOU KNOW WHAT YOU'RE SINGING TO?"
cards: A king holds a great sacrifice, and his singers take their places. Into the hall walks a ragged man. Not long before, in a famine, he was eating a stranger's leftover beans.
Now he sits down beside the king's chanters, and as they begin, he turns to each one: if you sing this without knowing the god it belongs to, your head will fall off. The singing stops.
His name is Ushasti, and the songs are the Sama Veda's. Today: the Veda as song.

teach.b: The Sama Veda is the Veda of melodies.

teach.h: "DO YOU KNOW THE GOD OF YOUR CHANT?"
teach.b: Saman means a chant, and its verses are ones that also appear in the Rig Veda, gathered and set to tune for the singers of the rite. It even opens with a call to the fire: agna a yahi vitaye, come, Agni, to the feast.
In the great rites some priests recited and others sang, led by the udgatri, the chief singer. Those are the singers Ushasti stops, in the Chandogya Upanishad, a text of the Sama Veda.
The king, alarmed, asks who he is, and hires him on the spot. Then the singers ask: so what are the gods of our chants? He tells them.
The opening chant belongs to breath, because every creature enters and leaves life with breath. The high chant belongs to the sun, because every creature sings to it when it rises high.
The response belongs to food, because every creature lives by taking it in. Breath, sun, food: what keeps you alive is what you're singing to.

teach.h: KNOWLEDGE AND FAITH MAKE IT STRONGER.
teach.b: Near its start the same Upanishad puts the teaching in one line: what is done with knowledge, with faith, and with its inner meaning becomes stronger. That's why Hindu tradition prizes melody and meaning together.
The tune carries the words in; knowing what they mean lets you sing them on purpose. A bhajan, an aarti, a mantra at a havan: sung knowing what it says, it is more than sound.

how: The Sama Veda is learned from a teacher by ear, melody and all, and in the Vedic rites its chants belong to the priests who sing; at home, many families sing aarti and bhajans, often in the evening.

games.q: what does “the sama veda as song” mean?
o: the Veda of melodies: hymn verses set to tune
a separate Veda of new words found nowhere else
a book of rules for building the fire altar

games.q: the Sama Veda and Ushasti — tap the pairs.
p: the man who stopped the king's singers

s: the Sama Veda brings a new set of words found nowhere else
its verses also appear in the Rig Veda. what the Sama Veda adds is the melody.
Ushasti told the singers the sound alone was enough
he warned them: sing without knowing the god of the chant, and your head will fall off.
the Chandogya says what's done with knowledge and faith becomes stronger
Chandogya 1.1.10: done with knowledge, with faith, with its inner meaning, it becomes stronger.

games.q: you're the king's chief singer. a stranger asks if you know the god of your chant. you don't. what does the story say to do?
o: keep singing; the sound is enough
stop, and learn what the chant is for
games.why: the singers stopped and asked Ushasti, and he taught them: breath, the sun, food. what's done with knowledge and faith is stronger.

practice: Choose one line you know by heart: an aarti, a bhajan, a mantra, or simply Om. Before you sing it, think for a moment about what it means; if you aren't sure, hold the one word you do know.
Then sing or hum it once, slowly, meaning it; if you can't make sound where you are, say it silently. If you don't pray, use a line from a song that matters to you.

wordCard.voice: The Sama Veda as song. Saman, melody: Rig Veda verses set to tune and, as Ushasti taught the king's singers, sung knowing what they're for. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a chant, a melody. The Sama Veda is the Veda of the samans.

carryVoice: Your line: the sama veda, sacred song, sung knowing what it means. Breath, sun, food. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sama Veda, opening verse (also Rig Veda 6.16.10)
Sama Veda as a whole (Rig Veda verses arranged for singing; the chanter priests of the rite)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.10–1.11 (Ushasti Chakrayana in the famine; he warns the prastotri, udgatri and pratihartri; the deities of the chants: breath, the sun, food)
Chandogya Upanishad 1.1.10 (what is done with knowledge, with faith, with the upanishad becomes more powerful)
